en: The Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Śramaṇa Kālodaka of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Long ago, during incalculable kalpas, the Bodhisattva was a king; his parents had passed away early.
He abdicated his kingdom in favor of his younger brother and renounced the world to seek the Way.
From afar he saw a Brahmin surnamed Gautama, and the Bodhisattva consequently studied the Way under that Brahmin.
The brahmin replied to the Bodhisattva, saying:
"Discard the royal garments you currently wear; braid your hair and knot *śāla* grass to make a robe such as the one I wear, and accept my Gautama clan name."

Thereupon the Bodhisattva accepted them; having clothed his body in these robes, he—of the Gautama clan—purified his will and entered the deep mountains, where amidst forests, thickets, and rugged precipices, he sat in meditation, mindful of the Way.
The brahmin said:
"You are a king who has long dwelt in noble status and have been spared from toil and hardship.
In summer you may drink water and eat various fruits and melons; [how can you endure such suffering?]"
"In winter, you may return to the cities and towns to beg for food among the streets and alleys.
Return to your place under the tree and practice meditative contemplation without fail.

When the Bodhisattva returned to his own kingdom with the alms he had collected, none throughout the entire nation—from the king above down to the common people—were able to recognize him as the Bodhisattva; they took him to be the Lesser Gautama.
The Bodhisattva had constructed a vihāra within a grove of sweet fruit trees outside the city walls, where he sat in solitude.

At that time, five hundred great bandits from the kingdom, having plundered official property and fled, passed by the side of the Bodhisattva’s hermitage; their tracks were scattered about, and their discarded belongings lay on both sides of the Bodhisattva’s dwelling.
The next day, when the bandits were being captured and those pursuing them discovered that their tracks led beneath the Bodhisattva’s house, they seized the Bodhisattva.
They brought him before the authorities and accused him of being a great thief in the kingdom who had committed successive acts of robbery; his crimes, they said, merited death.
The king then commanded his ministers:
"According to the law, such a person as this should have a wooden stake driven through his body.
He was set up as a great pillar; blood flowed from his body and streamed down to the ground.
The Great Gautama, perceiving this with his divine eye from deep within the mountains, flew there by means of his supernormal power and asked him:
"What crime have you committed that your suffering is so cruel?"
"The abscess surely causes painful injury; why do you endure such suffering?
The Bodhisattva replied, "While there is pain from the wound on the outside, within I harbor a heart of compassion."
"I do not know for what crime you have been so unjustly executed.
Mahāgautama said, "You have no children; who shall succeed you? Why do you endure such pain?"
The Bodhisattva replied, "My life lasts but a moment; why speak of descendants?
Thereupon, the king ordered his attendants to shoot him dead with powerful crossbows and flying arrows.
Mahāgautama, weeping with grief and shedding tears, lowered the corpse and enshrouded it in a coffin for burial.
Thereupon, he took the remaining blood from within the earth, formed it into lumps of clay, and each taking one, they placed them in the mountains on either side.
He returned to his vihāra; the blood from the left side adhered to the vessel on the left, and likewise for the right.
Mahāgautama said, "You are a practitioner of the Way; if your sincerity is true, the devas shall cause this blood to transform into human beings."
Ten months later, the left side became a male and the right side became a female; they were thus surnamed Gautama, and were named Śākyamuni and Śākyakalyāṇī respectively.
Since the beginning of the Bhadrakalpa, he first became the Śākya Tathāgata, whose lifespan was five million years;
the twenty-five kings who followed him had a lifespan of three million years;
King Mandhātṛ had a lifespan of one million years; and the Cakravartin kings—Mūrdhaja, Uposadha, and Aruṇa—all had a lifespan of one hundred thousand years.
From King Rājavatī (Joyful King) onwards, all kings lived for eighty-four thousand years.

From King Durmati (Evil Thought), who killed an ox as a sacrifice to the Cakravartin, he lost the golden wheel and obtained a silver wheel; he ruled over three continents and lived for ten thousand years.
King Dṛḍhamati (Firm Thought) made armor; he lived for five thousand years, obtained a copper wheel, and ruled over two continents, governing the southwest.
King Hṛṣṭavighāta lived for two thousand five hundred years and obtained an iron wheel, ruling over the southern continent.
This king had a crown prince who committed the five evils; for each instance of killing, his lifespan was reduced by one thousand years.
The ancients had nine afflictions:
cold, heat, hunger, thirst, birth, old age, illness, and death.
When Brahmins slaughter living beings for sacrificial offerings, from this arise four hundred and four illnesses.
From the time of King Siṃhacintin, the human lifespan gradually decreased until it reached one hundred and twenty years.

Following King Siṃhacintin came King Siṃhamati; during the reigns of eighty-four successive kings thereafter, the human lifespan diminished further, with people living for eighty, seventy, fifty, thirty, twenty, or even ten years.
Thereafter, there was a King of the Lion-Commander-Wheels named Śuddhodana, who was the father of the Bodhisattva.
Calculating from the beginning to the end of the Bodhisattva’s life, there were eighty-four thousand Cakravartin kings belonging to the Gautama clan, a family name of complete purity.
While the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven, desiring to descend to be born, he surveyed the world below to see in which kingdom he might take birth.
He said:
"Only in the house of King Śuddhodana may I manifest my birth."
Thereupon, in the heavens there was a tree named Tāla; as the Bodhisattva withdrew, he sat beneath another tree in contemplation, and the original tree no longer possessed its radiant splendor.
Then, a deva asked: "For what reason does the Bodhisattva abandon his original practice of sitting constantly and instead sit under another tree?
A son of heaven who knew the Bodhisattva’s intention replied to the deva:
"Do you not know? Now this Bodhisattva intends to descend to be born in Jambudvīpa; he observes which kingdom is suitable for his birth, and finds that only the house of Śuddhodana is fit."
Thereupon, all the devas said,
"Now that the Bodhisattva is descending to be born, what should we present as gifts?
Each devised a plan and said:

"O Pure and Luminous One, the four hundred and four kinds of jewels in the heavens are exquisitely carved and distinct, each with its own name and category; they all possess jewel-flowers, which serve as their vehicles."
The Naga King Elamatra provided a vehicle for him, a white elephant named Śvetagaja, whose fur and feathers were whiter than the White Snow Mountains.
The elephant had thirty-three heads, each head with seven tusks; upon each tusk was a pool, and upon each pool were seven blue lotuses (utpala), and upon each flower sat a jade maiden.
The Bodhisattva, together with eighty-four thousand sons of gods, descended riding upon a precious white elephant chariot.
At that time, while the Queen of King Śuddhodana was in a light sleep, she had a vision of a white elephant; she awoke in a state of startled alarm and informed the King of her dream.
The Bodhisattva’s father was named Śuddhodana; he had four brothers.
King Śuddhodana had two sons: the elder was named Siddhārtha, and the younger was named Nanda.
The Bodhisattva’s mother was named Māyā; Nanda’s mother was named Gautamī.
The Bodhisattva’s paternal uncle was named King Amṛtodana, who also had two sons: the elder son was named Devadatta, and the younger son was named Ānanda.
The middle younger brother of the Bodhisattva was named King Śuddhodana; he had two sons: the elder son was named Śākyamuni, and the younger son was Aniruddha.
The youngest younger brother of the Bodhisattva was named King Śuklodana; he had two sons: the elder son was named King Śākya, and the younger son was named King Śākyavarṇa.
The kingdom of Kapilavastu consisted of eight cities, with a total of nine million households.

Devadatta was born on the seventh day of the fourth month; the Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month; the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was born on the ninth day of the fourth month; and Ānanda was born on the tenth day of the fourth month.

The body of Devadatta was one zhang five chi four cun; the body of the Buddha was one zhang six chi; the body of Nanda was one zhang five chi four cun; and the body of Ānanda was one zhang five chi three cun.
The noble Śākyas were one chi and four cun tall; those of the other nations were all one chi and three cun tall.

The Bodhisattva’s maternal family was eight hundred li from the city; they belonged to the Gautama clan and were petty kings who ruled over a million households, known as the King of One Hundred Million.
The Bodhisattva’s wife was of the Gautama clan; she was the daughter of the Śākya elder named Jyotīrasa.
Her mother’s name was Candraprabhā.

There was a city situated near their residence; at the time of her birth, as the sun was about to set, its remaining radiance illuminated her home until the interior was filled with light. Consequently, she was named Gopī, which in the language of Jin means "Bright Woman."
Gopī was the first wife of the Prince; her father was the elder Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
The second wife of the Prince, who gave birth to Rāhula, was named Yaśodharā; her father was the elder Viśākha.
The third wife was named Mṛgajā; her father was the elder Śuddhodana.
Because he had three wives, the Prince’s father, the King, established for him palaces for the three seasons.

Each palace had twenty thousand court ladies; thus, across the three palaces, there were sixty thousand court ladies in total. Because the Prince was destined to become a Cakravartin King, sixty thousand court ladies were appointed for him.

The Buddha left home at the age of twenty-nine and attained the Way at thirty-five; from the eighth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the seventh month, sitting beneath a tree, constitutes one year.
In the second year, within the Deer Park, he preached the Dharma for Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others;
again, he preached the Dharma for Bimbapa and others;
and again, he preached the Dharma for seventeen people, including Kātyāyana and others.
Furthermore, he preached the Dharma for the great-talented elder and the two talented female lay disciples (upāsikā);
furthermore, he preached the Dharma for the nun Saṃprajānā;
furthermore, he preached the Dharma for the forty-two people during the time of the Buddha Tishya.
In the third year, he preached the Dharma for the three brothers, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his companions, with a full assembly of one thousand bhikṣus.
In the fourth year, on Mount Gajaśīrṣa, he preached the Dharma for the nāgas and spirits.
For five years, he taught the Dharma to Pṛthagvimala within the Bamboo Grove.
During those five years, before he had departed for Śrāvastī, Śāriputra was a brahmin with one hundred and twenty-five disciples, sitting beneath a tree.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana was serving as the Chancellor-General in the kingdom of Mithilā. While on an official journey, he saw Śāriputra sitting beneath a tree and asked him, "Why are you sitting here?"
Śāriputra replied, "I wish to study the Way.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"I wish for you to be my companion.
He then sent back his hundred officials and various ministers, retaining only one hundred and twenty-five men; with the two of them, there were thus two hundred and fifty people in total.
Śāriputra entered the city to beg for alms and saw the Buddha’s disciple, the bhikṣu Aśvajit.
He asked him, "For what reason do you, O practitioner of the Way, wear robes that are not like those of others?"
The horse trainer Bhikṣu replied,
"I am a disciple of the Buddha. Śāriputra asked:
"How does the Buddha teach the Dharma?
Aśvajit replied, "All phenomena arise from causes; through the cessation of conditions, all suffering is extinguished."
Thereupon, Śāriputra attained the stage of Srotāpanna; filled with joy, he returned and informed Maudgalyāyana, saying, "There are divine beings in this world."
Maudgalyāyana asked,
"How do you preach the Dharma?
Śāriputra explained the matter from beginning to end, and Maudgalyāyana immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The two men, together with their disciples, proceeded toward the Buddha's dwelling.
Before they had even arrived, the Buddha, having already known this in advance, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Two worthy gentlemen are now coming; one is named Bhikṣu Prajñāvat and the other is named Bhikṣu Ṛddhimat; they will arrive in a moment."
The Buddha preached the Four Noble Truths for him; Śāriputra attained Arhatship after seven days, while Maudgalyāyana attained it after fifteen days.

Six years later, Sudatta and Prince Jeta together built a vihāra for the Buddha, constructing twelve temple complexes, seventy-two lecture halls, three thousand six hundred rooms, and five hundred multi-storied pavilions.
In the seventh year, in the country of Aparagoyānī, he preached the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra* for eight people, including the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla.
In the eighth year, while at Mount Liucheng, he preached the Dharma for Tuṇḍila, the younger brother of King Candra.
In the ninth year, he preached the Dharma to Dharmaruci at the Śītavana Grove.
In the tenth year, he returned to the kingdom of Magadha and preached the Dharma to King Bimbisāra.
In the eleventh year, beneath the Tree of Fear, he expounded the *Pūrvayoga* for Maitreya.
In the twelfth year, returning to his father’s kingdom, he stayed at a retreat for the Śākyas located eighty *li* from the city and preached the Dharma to Kṣemaka;
subsequently, back in the capital, he preached the Dharma for his father the king and the Śākya clan, delivering eighty-four thousand people who attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
In these fourteen countries, the Buddha traveled, transformed beings, and preached the Dharma for twelve years.
Pōsìní Wáng (Prasenajit) means "Harmonious Joy" in the Jin language;
Jiāwéiyuè (Kapilavastu) means "Exquisite Virtue."
Śrāvastī means "possessing nothing that is not there" in the language of Jin;
Vaiśālī means "vast" in the language of Jin, and it is also known as "Transcending Birth and Death";
Rājagṛha means "King’s Abode City" in the language of Jin.
The kingdom of Kuru means "Land of the Wise" in the language of Jin;
Varanasi means "Deer Park" in the language of Jin, and is also called "Land of the Buddhas.
Within Jambudvīpa there are sixteen great kingdoms and eighty-four thousand cities, with eight kings and four celestial sons.
To the east is the Son of Heaven of Jin, whose people are flourishing;
to the south is the Son of Heaven of the kingdom of India, whose land abounds in famous elephants;
to the west is the Son of Heaven of the kingdom of Daqin, whose land is rich in gold, silver, jades, and gems.
To the northwest is the Heavenly King of the Yuezhi, whose territory abounds in fine horses.
Within his eighty-four thousand cities dwell people of six thousand four hundred kinds, with ten thousand varieties of sounds and fifty-six million billion hamlets.

There are six thousand four hundred species of fish, four thousand five hundred species of birds, two thousand four hundred species of beasts, ten thousand species of trees, eight thousand species of grasses, seven hundred and forty types of miscellaneous medicinal herbs, forty-three types of miscellaneous incenses, one hundred and twenty-one types of jewels, and seven types of primary jewels.

Within the ocean there are two thousand five hundred countries; one hundred and eighty of these countries consume the five grains, while three hundred and thirty countries consume fish, turtles, tortoises, and crocodiles.
There were five kings, each king presiding over five hundred cities.
The first king was named King of Srei; his entire territory served the Buddha and did not serve various heterodox deities.
The second king was named Kāla; his territory produced the seven treasures.
The third king was named Bala; his territory produced forty-two kinds of incense as well as white lapis lazuli.
The fourth king was named Jayā; his territory produced cardamom, costus, and black pepper.
The fifth king was named Nala; his territory produced white pearls and seven-colored lapis lazuli.
The inhabitants of the five great kingdoms and their cities are mostly dark-skinned, short, and small in stature.

They are separated by a distance of six million five hundred thousand *li*; beyond this point there is only the salt ocean with no human beings, extending for one million four hundred thousand *li* until reaching the Cakravāḍa Mountains.
The Sutra on the Twelve Wanderings Spoken by the Buddha.
